entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.1-1Chr.11.3">1Ch 11:1-3</reference> <hi type="italic">The anointing of David to be king over the whole of Israel in Hebron;</hi> cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.1">2Sa 5:1</reference>-3. - After Saul’s death, in obedience to a divine intimation, David left Ziklag, whither he had withdrawn himself before the decisive battle between the Philistines and the Israelites, and betook himself with his wives and his warriors to Hebron, and was there anointed by the men of Judah to be king over their tribe (<reference osisRef="2Sam.2.1-2Sam.2.4">2Sa 2:1-4</reference>). But Abner, the captain of Saul’s host, led Ishbosheth, Saul’s son, with the remainder of the defeated army of the Israelites, to Mahanaim in Gilead, and there made him king over Gilead, and gradually also, as he reconquered it from the Philistines, over the land of Israel, over Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all (the remainder of) Israel, with the exception of the tribal domain of Judah. Ishbosheth’s kingship did not last longer than two years, while David reigned over Judah in Hebron for seven years and a half (<reference osisRef="2Sam.2.10">2Sa 2:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.2.11">2Sa 2:11</reference>). When Abner advanced with Ishbosheth’s army from Mahanaim against Gibeon, he was defeated by Joab, David’s captain, so that he was obliged again to withdraw beyond Jordan (2 Sam 2:12-32); and although the struggle between the house of Saul and the house of David still continued, yet the house of Saul waxed ever weaker, while David’s power increased. At length, when Ishbosheth reproached the powerful Abner because of a concubine of his father’s, he threatened that he would transfer the crown of Israel to David, and carried his threat into execution without delay. He imparted his design to the elders of Israel and Benjamin; and when they had given their consent, he made his way to Hebron, and announced to David the submission of all Israel to his sway (2 Sam 3:1-21). Abner, indeed, did not fully carry out the undertaking; for on his return journey he was assassinated by Joab, without David’s knowledge, and against his will. Immediately afterwards, Ishbosheth, who had become powerless and spiritless through terror at Abner’s death, was murdered in his own house by two of the leaders of his army. There now remained of Saul’s family only Jonathan’s son Mephibosheth (<reference osisRef="2Sam.4.1-2Sam.4.12">2Sa 4:1-12</reference>), then not more than twelve years old, and lame in both his feet, and all the tribes of Israel determined to anoint David to be their king. The carrying out of this resolution is narrated in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.1-1Chr.11.3">1Ch 11:1-3</reference>, in complete agreement as to the facts with <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.1-2Sam.5.3">2Sa 5:1-3</reference>, where the matter has been already commented upon. In ch. 12 23-40 there follows a more detailed account of the assembly of the tribes of Israel in Hebron. The last words in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.3">1Ch 11:3</reference>, וגו יהוה כּדבר, are a didactic addition of the author of the Chronicle, which has been derived from <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.13">1Sa 16:13</reference> and 1Sa 15:28. In <reference osisRef="2Sam.5.4-2Sam.5.5">2Sa 5:4-5</reference>, in accordance with the custom of the author of the books of Samuel and Kings to state the age and duration of the reign of each of the kings immediately after the announcement of their entry upon their office, there follows after the preceding a statement of the duration of David’s reign; cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.1">1Sa 13:1</reference>; 2Sa 2:10., 1Ki 14:21; 1Ki 15:2, etc. This remark is to be found in the Chronicle only at the close of David’s reign; see <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.29">1Ch 29:29</reference>, which shows that Thenius’ opinion that this verse has been omitted from the Chronicle by a mistake is not tenable.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.10-1Chr.11.14">1Ch 11:10-14</reference> <hi type="italic">A register of the heroes</hi> who stood by him in the establishment of his kingdom. The greater part of this register is found in 2 Sam 23:8-39 also, though there are many divergences in the names, which for the most part have found their way into one or other of the texts by errors of transcription. The conclusion (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.41-1Chr.11.47">1Ch 11:41-47</reference> of the Chronicle) is not found in 2 Sam 23, either because the author of the Chronicle followed another and older register than that used by the author of the book of Samuel, or because the latter has not communicated all the names contained in his authority. The former of these is the more probable supposition. In the Chronicle the superscription of the register is enlarged by the insertion in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.10">1Ch 11:10</reference>, before the simple superscription in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11">1Ch 11:11</reference></hi>, cf. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Sam.23.8">2Sa 23:8</reference></hi>, of a further superscription informing us of the design which the chronicler had in introducing the register at this place. “These are the chiefs of David’s heroes who stood by him strongly (עם התחזּק, as <reference osisRef="Dan.10.21">Dan 10:21</reference>) in his kingdom, with the whole of Israel to make him king, according to the word of Jahve, over Israel.” The collocation הגּבּרים ראשׁי is accounted for by the fact that הגּבּור is a designation of a valiant or heroic man in general, without reference to his position, whether co-ordinate with or subordinate to others. Among David’s גּבּרים who helped to establish his kingdom, are not merely those who are mentioned by name in the following register, but also, as we learn from 1 Chron 12, the great number of valiant men of all the tribes, who, even during his persecution by Saul, crowded round him, and immediately after Saul’s death came to him in Hebron to hail him king. The enumeration in our passage contains only the chiefs, ראשׁים, of those valiant men, i.e., those who held the first rank among them, and who were in great part leaders in the army of David, or became so. להמליכו is not to be confined to the mere appointment to the kingship, but includes also his establishment in it; for there follows an account of the heroic deeds which the men enumerated by name performed in the wars which David waged against his enemies in order to maintain and increase his kingly power. יהוה דּבר יהוה .rewop concerning Israel is the word of the Lord, the import of which is recorded in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.3">1Ch 11:3</reference>, that David should feed His people Israel, and be ruler over them. The <hi type="italic">ipsissima verba</hi> are not found in the earlier history of David, but the substance of them has been deduced from <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.13">1Sa 16:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.28">1Sa 15:28</reference>; cf. herewith the remarks on 2Sa 3:18. The enumeration of these heroes is introduced in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11">1Ch 11:11</reference> by a short supplementary superscription, “these the number of the heroes.” That מספּר should be used instead of the שׁמות of Samuel is surprising, but is explained by the fact that these heroes at first constituted a corps whose designation was derived from their number. They originally amounted to thirty, whence they are still called the thirty, השּׁלשׁים; cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.12">1Ch 11:12</reference>, and the discussion on 2Sa 23:8. In both narratives three classes are distinguished. <div eID="gen5689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5690" type="x-p"/> Jashobeam, Eleazar, and Shammah hold the first place, and specially bold and heroic deeds performed by them are recorded, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11-1Chr.11.14">1Ch 11:11-14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.8">2Sa 23:8</reference>-12. For details as to themselves and their deeds, see on the last cited passage. There we have already remarked, that in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.13">1Ch 11:13</reference> of the text of the Chronicle, the three lines which in Samuel come between שׁם נאספוּ בּפּלשׁתּים (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.9">2Sa 23:9</reference>) and פלשׁתּים ויּעספוּ, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11">1Ch 11:11</reference>, have been, through wandering of the copyist’s eye, omitted; and with them the name of the third hero, שׁמּה, has also been dropped, so that the heroic deed done by him, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Chr.11.13">1Ch 11:13</reference></hi>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.14">1Ch 11:14</reference>, appears, according to our present text, to have been performed by Eleazar. In place of the words, “And the Philistines had gathered themselves together there to battle, and there was a parcel of ground full of barley,” <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.13">1Ch 11:13</reference>, the text, according to the narrative in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.11">2Sa 23:11</reference>, must have stood originally thus: “The Philistines had gathered themselves together there to battle, and the men of Israel went up (sc., retreating from the Philistines up the mountain); he, however, stood firm, and smote the Philistines till his hand was wearied, and cleaved unto the sword (i.e., clung crampedly to his sword through fatigue): there wrought Jahve a great deliverance on that day, and the people returned (from their flight) behind him only to spoil. And after him was Shammah the son of Aga the Hararite, and the Philistines had gathered themselves together to battle,” etc. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.14">1Ch 11:14</reference> the plural forms יתיצּבוּ, ויּצּילוּה, ויּכּוּ, are incorrect, and should be changed into singulars, as in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.12">2Sa 23:12</reference>, since only the deed of the hero Shammah is here spoken of. The plurals were probably introduced into the text after the missing lines had been dropped out by a reader or copyist, who, on account of the דּייד עם היה הוּא (<reference osisRef="1Chr.11.13">1Ch 11:13</reference>), understood the three clauses of <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.14">1Ch 11:14</reference> to refer to Eleazar and David. ויּושׁע, on the contrary, is here perfectly appropriate, and is not to be altered to suit the ויּעשׂ of Samuel, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.14">1Ch 11:14</reference>, for the καὶ ἐποίησε of the lxx is not of itself a sufficient reason for doing so.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.15-1Chr.11.19">1Ch 11:15-19</reference> <div eID="gen5690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5691" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.15-1Chr.11.19">1Ch 11:15-19</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.13-2Sam.23.17">2Sa 23:13-17</reference>) there follows an exploit of three others of the thirty, whose names have not been handed down. ראשׁ השּׁלושׁים, the thirty chiefs (not, as Thenius wrongly interprets the words, these three knights the chief parts, i.e., these three chief knights), are David’s heroes hereafter mentioned, the thirty-two heroes of the third class named in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.26-1Chr.11.40">1Ch 11:26-40</reference> (or vv. 24-39 of Samuel). That three others, different from the before-mentioned Jashobeam, Eleazar, and Shammah are intended, is plain from the omission of the article with שׁלושׁה; for if these three were spoken of, we would have השׁלושׁה, as in 1Ch 11:18. For further remarks on this exploit, which was probably performed in the war treated of in 1Ch 14:8., and in 2Sa 5:17., see on <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.13">2Sa 23:13</reference>-17. The words וגו האנשׁים הדם, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.19">1Ch 11:19</reference>, are to be translated, “The blood of these men shall I drink in their souls? for for their souls (i.e., for the price of their souls, at the risk of their life) have they brought it.” The expression “blood in their souls” is to be understood according to <reference osisRef="Gen.9.4">Gen 9:4</reference> and <reference osisRef="Lev.17.14">Lev 17:14</reference> (הוּא בנפשׁו דּמו, “his blood is in the soul,” is that which constitutes his soul). As there blood and soul are used synonymously (the blood as seat of and container of the soul, and the soul as floating in the blood), so here David, according to our account of his words, compares the water, which those heroes had brought for the price of their souls, to the souls of the men, and the drinking of the water to the drinking of their souls, and finally the souls to the blood, in order to express his abhorrence of such a draught. The meaning therefore may be thus expressed: “Shall I drink in this water the souls, and so the blood, of these men; for they have brought the water even for the price of their souls?”

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.20-1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:20-25</reference> <div eID="gen5691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5692" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.20-1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:20-25</reference> the second class of heroes, to which Abshai (Abishai) and Benaiah belonged, cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.18-2Sam.23.23">2Sa 23:18-23</reference>, is spoken of. They were not equal to the preceding three in heroic deeds, but yet stood higher than the list of heroes which follows in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.26">1Ch 11:26</reference> and onwards. אבשׁי, as <reference osisRef="1Chr.2.16">1Ch 2:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.10">2Sa 10:10</reference>, while in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.18">2Sa 23:18</reference> and elsewhere he is called אבישׁי, was one of the three sons of Zeruiah (<reference osisRef="1Chr.2.16">1Ch 2:16</reference>). It is difficult to explain השׁלושׁה ראשׁ, “he was the chief of the three,” instead of which we find in <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.23">2Sa 23:23</reference> השׁלשׁי, i.e., השּׁלשׁי, “chief of the body-guard” (knights). But owing to the succeeding שׁם (ולו) בּשּׁלושׁה ולא, where Samuel also has בּשּׁלשׁה, and to the recurrence of השׁלושׁה on two occasions in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.21">1Ch 11:21</reference> (cf. 2 <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.19">2Sa 23:19</reference>), it does not seem possible to alter the text with Thenius. Bertheau proposes to get rid of the difficulty by taking the word שׁלושׁה in two different significations-on the one hand as denoting the numeral three, and on the other as being an abstract substantive, “the totality of the thirty.” He justifies the latter signification by comparison of <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.21">1Ch 11:21</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:25</reference>, and of <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.19">2Sa 23:19</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.23">1Ch 11:23</reference>, from which he deduces that שׁלושׁה and שׁלושׁים denote a larger company, in which both Abishai and Benaiah held a prominent place. But this signification cannot be made good from these passages. In both clauses of <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:25</reference> (and <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.23">2Sa 23:23</reference>) השּׁלשׁים and השּׁלשׁה are contrasted, which would rather go to prove the contrary of Bertheau’s proposition, viz., that השּׁלשׁה, the three, cannot at the same time denote the whole of the thirty, השּׁלשׁים. The truth of the matter may be gathered from a comparison of <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.18">1Ch 11:18</reference> with 1Ch 11:15. In <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.18">1Ch 11:18</reference> השּׁלשׁה is synonymous with השּׁלושׁים מן השׁלושׁה, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.15">1Ch 11:15</reference>; i.e., the three in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.18">1Ch 11:18</reference> are the same men who in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.15">1Ch 11:15</reference>, where they are first met with, are called three of the thirty; and consequently השּׁלשׁה, the three (triad), <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.21">1Ch 11:21</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:25</reference>, can only denote the triad of heroes previously named. This is placed beyond doubt by a comparison of <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.24">1Ch 11:24</reference> with <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:25</reference>, since the הגּבּרים שׁלושׁה, the triad of heroes, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.24">1Ch 11:24</reference>, corresponds to the simple השּׁלשׁה of 1Ch 11:25. The only remaining question is, whether by this triad of heroes we are to understand those spoken of in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.11-1Chr.11.14">1Ch 11:11-14</reference>, - Jashobeam, Eleazar, and Shammah, - or the three whose names are not given, but whose exploit is narrated in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.15">1Ch 11:15</reference>-19. But the circumstance that the names of the three latter are not mentioned goes decidedly to show that השּׁלשׁה in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.20-1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:20-25</reference> does not denote that nameless triad, whose exploit is manifestly adduced incidentally only as a similar case, but the three most valiant, who held the first rank among David’s heroes. Bertheau’s opinion, that in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.20-1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:20-25</reference> one triad of heroes is distinguished from another, cannot be regarded as well-founded, for the three of whom Abishai was chief are not distinguished, and are not different from the three to whom, according to <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.21">1Ch 11:21</reference>, he did not attain. Nor is there greater reason to believe that the triad of <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.20">1Ch 11:20</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.21">1Ch 11:21</reference> is different from that in <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.24">1Ch 11:24</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.25">1Ch 11:25</reference>, among whom Benaiah made himself a name, and to whom he did not attain. The fact of being chief or prince over the three is not irreconcilably contradictory to the statement that he did not attain to them, i.e., did not come up to them in heroic strength, as is shown by the two classes being connected in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="1Chr.11.21">1Ch 11:21</reference></hi>. As to the rank which the triad held in the regular forces of David, we know nothing further than that Jashobeam was, according to <reference osisRef="1Chr.27.2">1Ch 27:2</reference>, leader of that part of the army which was on duty during the first month. Eleazar the son of Dodo, and the Hararite Shammah the son of Aga, are not mentioned anywhere but in our list. Abishai, on the contrary, who had already distinguished himself by his audacious courage in David’s struggle with Saul (1Sa 26:6.), conducted together with Joab the war against Abner (2 Sam 2:24-3:30). Afterwards, in David’s war with the Ammonites, he was under Joab in command of the second half of the host (2Sa 10:10.); in the war against Absalom he commanded a third part of the host (1Ch 18:2.); and in the struggle with the rebel Sheba he commanded the vanguard of the royal troops sent against the rebel (1Ch 20:6.); and in general held, along with Joab the commander-in-chief, the first place among David’s captains. In this position he was chief of the three heroes before mentioned, and their leader (שׂר), and among them had made himself a name. ולא, <reference osisRef="1Chr.11.20">1Ch 11:20</reference>, is an orthographical error for ולו, as in fifteen other passages, according to the Masora. See on <reference osisRef="Exod.21.10">Exo 21:10</reference> and Isa 63:9.
